overview: The Wausau Infrastructure and Facilities Committee held a lengthy meeting dominated by public testimony from boulevard street residents demanding a return to the decades-old practice of plowing snow toward center medians rather than toward curbs. The committee voted to table the snow plowing policy decision until August, directing staff to return with cost estimates for outfitting plow equipment with left-side wings. Other actions included approving a transportation project plat, setting two public hearings on alley/road vacations, approving a public art sculpture, renewing a stormwater memorandum, and approving a rectangular rapid flashing beacon at Thomas Street while rejecting one at Golden Meadow Street.

discussions.item: Snow plowing policy on boulevard streets
discussions.body: Ten members of the public spoke, representing Oaklair Boulevard, Highland Park Boulevard, and other southeast side boulevard streets, all urging the committee to reverse a policy change made roughly two years ago that shifted snow plowing from center medians to outer curbs. Alder Carol Lukkins presented a petition signed by over 40 property owners and read testimony from residents unable to attend. Public works staff explained that current equipment has right-side wings only, that plowing contraflow to push snow to the median would violate state law and expose drivers to personal liability, and that adding left-side wings to the two loader routes would cost an estimated $40,000–$50,000 per machine. A committee member noted that staff had confided no formal study was conducted before the policy change. Alder Slonsky's written statement, read into the record, urged the committee to maintain the current outside-curb policy. No motion to reverse the policy was made; instead the committee by motion agreed to bring the issue back in August with cost estimates for equipment upfitting and guidelines for handling future exception requests.

discussions.item: South 52nd/East Wausau Avenue Transportation Project Plat (Project ID 699-Z00-01)
discussions.body: Staff presented this Wisconsin DOT-led connecting highway project, now at approximately 70% design, requiring approval of a transportation project plat to authorize a real estate professional to secure necessary easements and small property takings from affected homeowners. Staff recommended approval and the committee voted unanimously in favor with no notable debate.

discussions.item: Preliminary resolution to set public hearing: alley vacation bounded by Lake View Drive, Bertha Street, Elmwood Boulevard, and Midway Boulevard
discussions.body: Staff explained that a valid petition had been received and that this motion would only set a public hearing where neighbors could testify for or against the vacation before the committee votes on it. The motion passed unanimously with minimal discussion.

discussions.item: Approve sculpture at southeast corner of Third Street and Washington Street
discussions.body: Staff noted the arts commission approved the sculpture 4-1 and forwarded it to the infrastructure committee because the sculpture would be placed in the city right-of-way, requiring an encroachment permit with insurance. A committee member asked whether the sculpture would obstruct sight lines; staff said engineering would make a final placement determination. The sculpture is entirely funded by the private owner (Foundry), who retains ownership. The motion to approve and forward to the city attorney for an encroachment agreement passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Renewal of stormwater memorandum of agreement with surrounding communities
discussions.body: Staff briefly described the agreement, under which Marathon County operates storm sewer facilities in surrounding communities in compliance with local ordinances and MS4 requirements. The committee approved renewal unanimously with no debate.

discussions.item: Preliminary resolution to set public hearing: vacation of a portion of Liberty Ridgeway
discussions.body: A petition was received from the property owner at the end of Liberty Ridgeway seeking to vacate a small stub portion, with staff noting development plans in the area had changed and a large home is under construction nearby. The motion to set the public hearing passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Developing preliminary engineering plans for Wausau Center urban design and transportation master plan
discussions.body: Staff proposed seeking approximately $150,000 in the 2027 budget for 30% preliminary engineering plans to begin implementing the 2019 Wausau Center urban design plan, which became more actionable after state highway designations for Highways 51 and 52 were removed from downtown in 2024. Committee members discussed converting one-way streets to two-way, a potential roundabout at Grand Avenue and Forest Street, and a protected bike lane on Forest Street, with concerns raised about outdated traffic counts, increased downtown development since 2019, and budget priorities. One member moved to explore preliminary engineering plans but the motion died for lack of a second, with one member stating they were not ready to commit funding given current budget pressures.

discussions.item: Rectangular rapid flashing beacon at East Thomas Street pedestrian crossing west of McClary Street
discussions.body: Staff recommended approval, noting the crossing met all RRFB criteria except minimum pedestrian count thresholds, but that observers recorded extremely long wait times for pedestrians, suggesting the newer River Edge Trail Extension discourages crossing use. The bicycle and pedestrian advisory committee supported it. One member asked about lower-cost alternatives; staff said a pedestrian refuge island and high-visibility signage already exist and few other options remain. The motion passed, though one member voted no, stating that at $15,000–$20,000 other options should be exhausted first.

discussions.item: Rectangular rapid flashing beacon at Stevens Drive and Golden Meadow Street
discussions.body: Unlike the Thomas Street item, staff did not support this RRFB, noting traffic volumes and pedestrian counts were lower and field staff observed no conflicts or extended crossing waits. The bicycle and pedestrian advisory committee recommended it, prompted by a resident letter describing near-miss incidents. A committee member moved to table it until October for more accurate pedestrian counts when school is in session; another member declined to second the motion, saying they were not convinced even then that this location would be the priority on Stevens Drive over the West Wausau Avenue intersection. The motion died for lack of a second and no action was taken.

publicComment: Ten speakers addressed the committee. Jim Wearerig (2408 Oakwood Boulevard) described safety hazards from snow banks blocking sight lines and storm drains under the current plowing policy. Karen Briggs (154 Oaklair Boulevard, 51-year resident) argued the old plowing method worked for decades and that residents on shared driveways cannot park on the street under current conditions. Jean Krooks (119 Oaklair Boulevard) described sight-line dangers and impossibility of two-way travel on the 100 block. Jean Rolki (146 Oaklair Boulevard) added concerns about garbage pickup difficulties, tipping carts, and boulevard trees dying from lack of snowmelt moisture. Jonathan Smith (1114 Prospect Avenue) supported both the Wausau Center urban design plan and the Thomas Street RRFB, noting he sometimes waits two to three minutes to cross Thomas Street. Alder Carol Lukkins (725 Ethos Street) presented a formal request on behalf of southeast side boulevard residents citing a 40-plus-signature petition and documented safety hazards, asking the committee to direct public works to resume plowing toward center medians on five named boulevards. Alder Sarah Watson (412 North Fifth Avenue) read a letter from constituent Eric Locoman (1409 Golden Meadow Street) requesting an RRFB at Stevens Drive and Golden Meadow Street, citing near-miss incidents and a curved roadway limiting driver sight lines in a school zone. Danielle Fischer (1212 Highland Park Boulevard) brought a neighbor's broken mailbox as a physical exhibit of damage caused by the new plowing policy and said every household on Highland Park Boulevard signed a petition for reversion. Felix Gallow (126 Highland Park Boulevard) recounted a detailed conversation with public works superintendent Dustin in which Gallow said Dustin acknowledged no formal study was done before the policy change, that the equipment can plow to either side, and that the real motivation was an inability to manage numerous exception requests citywide. Courtney Olen (1206 Highland Park Boulevard) argued the entire neighborhood was unified across political lines in wanting the policy reversed.
